title: Edge protection, floor openings and covers
audience: Workers, leading hands and supervisors who set up or check edge controls, openings and covers on trade and exterior work.
learningOutcomes: Identify when edge protection is needed, and what it must do.
Check a guardrail system for height, rails, toe board, fixing and strength before use.
Cover or guard an opening so that it cannot be stepped into or fallen through.
Decide when a warning line or a restraint is used, and what neither of them can do.

instruction.heading: Why the edge and the opening come first
instruction.body: A physical edge or opening control removes the need for each worker to make a correct decision every minute. The sources in this pack list open sides and edges, holes, wall openings, skylights, concrete forms with exposed reinforcement, excavations and walkways as places where protection is needed. Treat any unprotected side near the work as an active fall exposure until it has been controlled.

instruction.heading: What a guardrail system must do
instruction.body: A guardrail system is a top rail, a mid-rail and a toe board. Guardrail heights and loads are set out in the sources, and the figures they give are not Australian. The mid-rail sits halfway up between the top rail and the working surface, and the toe board stops materials sliding off. The top rail is expected to resist a push at any spot on its upper edge, and the mid-rail a push along its length, without failing. The control holds whatever the figure: the rail must be complete, fixed, at the right height, able to stop a body pushing against it, and inspected before first use and after any impact.

instruction.heading: Covering an opening
instruction.body: An opening is a gap in a floor, roof, deck or wall. Cover it with a cover that is secured against wind and against being moved, and mark it clearly. Before any cover is removed, barricade the area so that no one steps into the opening. Skylights and roof lights are openings too, and they need a rail or a strong cover. Wall openings at height need a guardrail, a barrier or another fall control.

instruction.heading: Warning lines and restraint
instruction.body: A warning line is a marked rope, chain or line, fixed a set distance back from an edge. It warns people. It does not stop a fall. One source says that anyone working between the line and the edge needs a harness and an arrest system. A thin rope on its own does not guard an edge: one source judges a single nylon rope to be an improper guard for an open floor, and the same logic applies to tape or light cord that a person can step over or pull down. Restraint lines, where used, stop a worker reaching the edge, and their anchor and length must be checked under “Fall protection and arrest systems”.

instruction.heading: Nets, mesh and fixed barriers
instruction.body: A safety net catches a person who falls. It must be placed as close as practical below the work, and installed and checked by a competent individual. Use a net where a guardrail cannot be installed, and check it before each installation and again after it. Mesh or toe boards fitted to a rail also stop small materials falling.

instruction.heading: Protruding steel and excavation edges
instruction.body: Protruding reinforcing steel and the unprotected ends of scaffold tubes create a fall and impalement hazard. Cap or cover each end before work near it. Excavations with straight sides and an unprotected drop also need protection. For trenches, the national excavation code from Safe Work Australia (2015) says a trench 1.5 metres or deeper needs its walls held up by supports, benching or battering, wherever a cave-in could bury a person, whatever the depth (national model code; state adoption to be checked). Where workers must stand close to an unprotected excavation edge, they need a restraint or lifeline arrangement.

instruction.heading: Keeping the controls in place
instruction.body: Do not remove an edge control to pass a tool or a material through. If a control must come down for a task, plan a temporary replacement control, record the reason, and get the supervisor's sign-off before the work starts. Put the control back as soon as the task allows, and inspect it again.

procedure: List each unprotected side, edge, opening and protruding hazard in the work area.
Choose the control for each, in this order: guardrail or barrier first, then cover, then warning line with restraint, then net, then fall arrest.
Check the rail system: height, rails, toe board, fixings and strength.
Cover and mark each opening, and barricade it before any cover is removed.
Cap or cover each protruding steel or tube end.
Use a warning line only where people are not exposed to the edge without fall arrest.
Inspect each control before first use, and after any impact or change.
Remove a control only with a replacement control and a supervisor's sign-off.

workedExamples.situation: A deck builder must work beside a deck edge that has no balustrade yet, about one metre above the lawn.
workedExamples.reasoning: A temporary guardrail or edge barrier is the first option, with a restraint or arrest system as the fallback. A warning line on its own does not protect the worker. The install sequence should be changed so that the guardrail goes in before the edge is worked on, and people are kept off the edge.

workedExamples.situation: A roofer must clean a skylight, and the cover that is in place is light and not fixed down.
workedExamples.reasoning: No. A cover that wind or foot pressure can lift or shift is not secure. Fix the cover, mark it, or guard the opening with a rail before work starts. The skylight is not left to a light cover while the work proceeds nearby.

equipmentAndPpe: Guardrail components: a toe board, a mid-rail and a top rail
Secured covers for openings, with markers
Warning-line posts and a clearly marked line
Safety netting where it is specified
Caps or covers for protruding steel and tube ends

commonErrors.error: Using tape or a light rope as an edge guard.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a rigid guardrail or a solid barrier. Tape warns; it does not guard.

commonErrors.error: Fitting a cover that is not secured.
commonErrors.prevention: Fix the cover, and test that it stays put under foot pressure.

commonErrors.error: Removing a rail for convenience and not refitting it.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not remove a rail. If removal cannot be avoided, plan a replacement and get sign-off.

commonErrors.error: Leaving reinforcing steel ends uncapped beside the work.
commonErrors.prevention: Cap or cover each protruding end before work near it begins.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Warning: a warning line is not an edge control. A person who works between the line and the edge must be on an arrest system.
Warning: an uncovered opening must be covered, guarded or barricaded before any work near it starts.

The guardrail heights and loads, the cover load, the net drop distance, the excavation trigger and the wall-opening height figure come from non-Australian sources, so check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.
The national falls code is listed for falls at workplaces (see “What counts as height work and how falls happen”).
Licence notice: this lesson does not grant a licence or authority to install or inspect fall-protection systems or nets. The sources say nets are installed and checked by a competent individual.

qualityStandard: Every unprotected edge and opening is listed and controlled before work starts.
Guardrail components are checked for height, rails, toe board and fixing.
A removed control is replaced and signed off before work proceeds.
documentationEvidence: Edge and opening control check record
Replacement control record where a rail or cover was removed
summary: A rigid edge control comes before a warning line, and a warning line never stops a fall.
Check a guardrail for height, rails, toe board, fixing and strength before use.
Cover, fix and mark every opening, and barricade before a cover is lifted.
Replace any control taken down, and get sign-off before the work continues.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about a warning line is correct?
options: It stops a fall and it protects the workers on the roof for the whole day and the job after it
It warns people but does not stop a fall; a person between the line and the edge needs fall arrest.
It can replace a guardrail on any roof and it is cheaper to fit and remove on any job
It is needed only for work close to the ground and not for any work on the roof at all

knowledgeChecks.question: An opening in a floor has a cover that moves when stepped on. What should happen?
options: Use it anyway for quick access and the cover is not needed for the job
Secure the cover, mark it, and barricade before removal; a loose cover is not used.
Stand the cover on its edge and leave it there for the day while the crew works
Leave the opening open for ventilation and put the cover back loosely on top

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about the guardrail figures in the sources is correct for Australia?
options: The figures are confirmed Australian standards and they apply to every site in the country and every trade in it at all times
The figures come from non-Australian sources and have not yet been confirmed; the control must still be complete, fixed and at a sound height.
The sources say guardrails are not needed on any roof that is flat, low, easy to walk on, close to the ground and dry
Only the toe board matters and nothing else about the guardrail or the fixings matters for the roof edge work at all today

officialReferences.title: Working at heights (Safe Work Australia)
officialReferences.covers: Read through a summary tool (WebFetch). Gives an order of preference for fall controls: do the work on the ground or a solid construction where possible; then a fall prevention device such as barriers, scaffolding or elevating work platforms; then a work positioning system; then a fall arrest system such as a safety net or catch platform. Refers to the model Code of Practice Managing the risk of falls at workplaces for more detail, which was not read in this pass. Does not give edge-protection, guardrail or warning-line heights, does not mention warning lines, and does not say who installs nets.
